## 1 Minute Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/1-minute-typing-test.html

Test your typing speed in exactly 60 seconds. This one minute typing test measures your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy — the standard quick check most typing sites use.

## 1 minute typing test
The 1 minute typing test is the most popular way to check typing speed. Sixty seconds is long enough to measure your real speed and short enough to fit into any break. Type the passage as fast as you can without mistakes — the test counts your WPM, accuracy and errors automatically. When the minute is up, your result appears instantly and is saved in this browser so you can compare it with your next attempt.
## Why 60 seconds?
A one minute test balances two things: it is long enough that a single lucky or unlucky sentence does not dominate the result, and short enough that you stay focused the whole time. Shorter tests such as 15 or 30 seconds are fun for quick bursts, but a 60 second test is what most people mean when they say typing speed. Recruiters and typing certificates almost always use a one minute test.
## What your 1 minute score means
Under 30 WPM marks a beginner still building touch typing foundations; 30 to 40 is typical for casual typists, and 40 to 60 covers the average adult range where most office work feels comfortable. Above 60 you are faster than roughly three quarters of test takers, 80-plus is professional territory for transcription and data entry, and anything past 100 approaches competitive speeds. Whatever your number, compare it against the benchmarks in our average typing speed guide rather than judging by a single lucky round.
## Typing test FAQ
A 60-second timed round: type the passage shown for exactly one minute, then get your WPM, accuracy and error breakdown instantly. One minute is the most-quoted test length, so scores compare directly across sites and job requirements.
Correct characters divided by 5, divided by the one elapsed minute. Because the test lasts exactly sixty seconds the maths is simple: 300 correct characters equals 60 WPM. The results panel shows both raw WPM and net WPM with errors subtracted.

## 2 Minute Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/2-minute-typing-test.html

Test your typing speed over 2 minutes — long enough for a stable WPM score, short enough to stay sharp. A great middle ground between the quick 1 minute test and the full 5 minute test.

## 2 minute typing test
The 2 minute typing test is a popular middle-ground length. Two minutes is long enough that your score reflects real typing speed rather than one lucky sentence, yet short enough to keep full concentration. Type the passage as fast and accurately as you can — WPM, accuracy and errors are counted automatically.
## 1 minute vs 2 minute vs 5 minute
A 1 minute test is a quick check, a 2 minute test is a reliable everyday measure, and a 5 minute test is best for serious benchmarking. If you are practising daily, the 2 minute test is a comfortable default that balances speed feedback and stability.
## Why a 2-minute typing test
Two minutes is the sweet spot between a quick sprint and a full endurance run. It's long enough to settle into a steady rhythm and smooth out a shaky start, yet short enough to retake several times in a sitting. Many employer screening tests use a two-minute format, which makes it ideal practice for job applications.
## A daily 2 minute practice routine
One reliable routine: open the test at the same time each day, take exactly two rounds with a one-minute stretch break between them, and keep the better score. Two rounds a day is enough to show a trend within a fortnight — most steady practicers gain 5 to 10 WPM in the first month. When progress stalls for a full week, switch to targeted drills for your slowest keys instead of adding more test rounds; our typing tips explain how to find them.
## 2 minute typing test vs 1 minute and 3 minute
Two minutes is the shortest round where a single bad sentence stops dominating the score. A 1 minute typing test can swing 10-15 WPM on one unfamiliar sentence; across two minutes that swing halves.
1 minute - good for daily speed checks and quick warm-ups.
2 minutes - the sweet spot for a repeatable score you can track week to week.
3 minute / 5 minute - endurance and technique, used for screening.
If you are tracking progress, keep the length fixed. Comparing a 2 minute score against a 5 minute score tells you about endurance, not improvement.

## 5 Minute Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/5-minute-typing-test.html

Measure your sustained typing speed over a full 5 minutes. A longer test averages out lucky bursts and fatigue, giving a more reliable words per minute (WPM) score than a quick 1 minute test.

## 5 minute typing test
The 5 minute typing test is the best way to measure your real, sustained typing speed. Over five minutes your score settles down: a single fast or slow sentence no longer dominates the result, and natural fatigue is factored in. This is why many employers and typing certifications prefer a 3-5 minute test over a 60 second one.
## Who should use a 5 minute test?
If you type for a living — data entry, transcription, programming, customer support — the 5 minute test reflects your working speed far better than a short burst. Take it a few times a week and watch your WPM and accuracy trend in the saved history below.
## Build typing endurance
A five-minute test measures something a quick sprint can't: how well you hold speed and accuracy as your hands tire. Pace yourself, keep your posture relaxed and your wrists level, and breathe. Finishing strong on the five-minute test is a reliable sign your typing is ready for long real-world sessions of writing, coding or data entry.
## How to prepare for the 5 minute test
Treat a five-minute attempt like a short workout: sit with feet flat and wrists floating level with the keyboard, roll your shoulders once, then run a 1 minute typing test as a warm-up. Keep water nearby but skip coffee right before — caffeine jitters tend to show up as extra errors around minute three. During the round, breathe steadily and use sentence breaks as micro-rests for your eyes. Two prepared attempts a week beat seven tired ones.
## 5 minute typing test: what a longer round reveals
Short tests measure reflexes; a 5 minute typing test measures technique. Most errors that show up here are not typos but fatigue patterns: the left hand drifts off home row, the pinky stops reaching for shift, and accuracy falls before speed does.
Speed decay - the WPM you hold at minute four is your working speed. Warm-up speed is not.
Accuracy drift - watch whether accuracy falls over time. If it does, slow down rather than push.
Rhythm breaks - long pauses cluster around punctuation and capitals, which is where drills pay off most.
Best practice once you have a baseline: run 1 minute typing tests daily for speed, and a 5 minute round weekly to confirm the speed is sustainable.
## Typing test FAQ
Yes. Longer tests average out short bursts of speed and moments of fatigue, so a 5 minute result is more stable and representative of your true typing speed than a 15 or 60 second test.
40 WPM is average, 60+ WPM is good, and 80+ WPM is professional level. Maintaining high accuracy over 5 minutes matters more than peak speed.

## Capital Letter Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/capital-letter-typing-test.html

Practise uppercase letters and the Shift key with a focused capital letter typing test. Build muscle memory for capitals and symbols while tracking your WPM and accuracy.

## Capital letter typing test
Capitals slow most people down because they need the Shift key and a return to the home row. This capital letter typing test gives you sentences full of proper nouns and uppercase words so you can drill the motion until it feels natural. Your WPM and accuracy are shown instantly after every run.
## How to type capitals faster
Use the opposite hand: press the Shift key with the hand that is not typing the letter. Keep your fingers on the home row and avoid using Caps Lock for single capitals. A few minutes of daily practice with this typing test makes the Shift reach automatic.
## Mastering the Shift key
Capital letters are where many typists lose speed. Reaching for Shift with the opposite hand — left Shift for right-hand letters and right Shift for left-hand letters — keeps your typing balanced and quick. This test mixes capitals through natural sentences so the Shift reach becomes second nature instead of a stumble.
## Capitalization in real writing
Every sentence starts with a capital, and names, places and titles add many more. Practising proper capitalization trains the timing of pressing Shift and a letter together smoothly, so your names and sentence starts flow without the tiny pauses that quietly drag down your words-per-minute.
## Frequently asked questions
It is a typing test that focuses on uppercase letters and the Shift key, so you can practise capitals, proper nouns and symbols rather than only lowercase words.
Capitals need a Shift key press with the opposite hand plus a quick return to the home row, which breaks your rhythm until the motion becomes muscle memory.
Yes. Free with no sign up, and your Shift-key drill results stay in your own browser.
Always Shift for single capitals: hold it with the opposite hand's pinky while the other hand strikes the letter. Caps Lock is only for multi-letter acronyms, and reaching for it mid-sentence breaks rhythm and costs accuracy.

## English Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/english-typing-test.html

Test your English typing speed with real sentences. Measure your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

## English typing test
An English typing test measures how fast and accurately you type English text. Your result is shown in WPM (words per minute), where every 5 characters counts as one word. Typing full English sentences — with punctuation and capitals — is the most realistic way to measure everyday typing speed.
## How to improve English typing
Practise with real sentences rather than isolated words, keep your fingers on the home row (ASDF JKL;), and look at the screen instead of the keyboard. Accuracy first, then speed: 10-15 focused minutes a day beats long occasional sessions.
## Practising English typing
This English typing test uses natural, everyday sentences rather than random letters, so you practise the real word patterns and spacing you meet in emails, essays and chat. Typing whole phrases trains the common letter pairs — "th", "ing", "and", "tion" — that make fluent English typing feel effortless.
## Why common words speed you up
A small set of words makes up most of what we write in English. Drilling high-frequency words like the, and, that, with and your builds instant muscle memory for the keystrokes you repeat thousands of times a day. Master those and your overall WPM rises across every kind of text you type.
## Typing test FAQ
Yes. The English typing test is free with no sign up, and your English WPM history is saved only in this browser.
40 WPM is average, 60-70 WPM is good, and 80+ WPM is professional level for most office and writing work.
The standard 5-characters-per-word rule, applied to real English sentences. Because English words average close to 5 characters, the formula matches real English text well; errors are subtracted for net WPM.
Slightly: WPM counts five characters as one word, and common English words average just under five, so scores on real sentences run a touch higher than on random-word drills. The difference is small — a few WPM — and consistent, so scores compare fairly.

## Spanish Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/spanish-typing-test.html

Test your Spanish typing speed with real Spanish sentences. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

## Spanish typing test
A Spanish typing test measures how fast and accurately you type Spanish text. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word. Typing full Spanish sentences — with accents, the letter ñ and inverted punctuation — is the most realistic way to measure everyday Spanish typing speed.
## How to improve Spanish typing
Practise with real sentences rather than isolated words, keep your fingers on the home row, and look at the screen instead of the keyboard. Spanish adds accented vowels (á, é, í, ó, ú) and ñ, so slow down at first to learn those key positions; accuracy first, then speed.
## Practising Spanish typing
This Spanish typing test uses natural, everyday sentences rather than random letters, so you practise the real word patterns of Spanish — common endings like -ción, -mente and -ando — together with the accented characters and ¿ ¡ punctuation you meet in real Spanish writing.
## Why accented characters matter
Accents in Spanish change a word's meaning (for example sí meaning yes versus si meaning if), so typing them correctly is part of typing Spanish well. Drilling sentences that include á, é, í, ó, ú and ñ builds muscle memory for the extra keystrokes, and your overall Spanish typing speed rises across every kind of text you write.

Yes. The Spanish typing test is free with no sign up; your Spanish results stay in this browser.
Yes. The practice sentences are real Spanish, so they include accented vowels (á, é, í, ó, ú), the letter ñ, and inverted ¿ ¡ punctuation.

No: the test accepts standard keystrokes and guides you through accented characters with the on-screen keyboard. A Spanish layout helps at speed, but beginners can start on any keyboard immediately.

## Typing Speed Test
This is a free online typing speed test. It measures how many words per minute (WPM) you can type and how accurate you are. The test works on any device with a keyboard — desktop, laptop, tablet or phone. There is nothing to install and no account needed.
## How to improve your typing speed
Take a short test every day. Start with a 1 minute typing test, then try 2 or 5 minutes as you get faster. Focus on accuracy first — speed follows accuracy. Keep your fingers on the home row and look at the screen, not the keyboard. Switch to quotes or numbers mode to practice punctuation and digits, which are the most common slowdowns.
## What is a good typing speed?
An average typing speed is about 40 WPM. Typing at 60 WPM is faster than most people and good for most office work. Above 80 WPM is fast, and professional typists and developers often reach 90–120 WPM. Children usually start around 20–30 WPM and improve quickly with a few minutes of daily practice.
Level | Typing speed
Average adult | 40-50 WPM
Good (office standard) | 60-80 WPM
Fast (top ~10%) | 80-100 WPM
Advanced (top ~1%) | 100+ WPM
These are rough bands - see the full average typing speed benchmarks by age and profession.

An online typing speed test gives you an instant, objective picture of how well you type. Instead of guessing, you get a clear WPM score and an accuracy percentage after every attempt. ## Choose your typing test duration and text
Everyone types differently, so this typing speed test lets you pick the length and style that suit you. You can also switch between sentences, famous quotes, numbers and common words, so you train exactly the keys you struggle with most.

Improvement is easier to see when you measure it. After each typing speed test your result is saved in your own browser, building a private history of WPM, accuracy and error counts. Watching those numbers climb week by week is motivating and tells you whether to push for raw speed or to slow down and tighten up accuracy. Your typing history stays private in your browser.
## Tips to type faster and more accurately
Fast typing is built on good habits. Keep your fingers on the home row, use all ten fingers, and glance at the screen rather than the keyboard. Take a typing test every day for ten to fifteen minutes and always value accuracy over raw speed, because fixing mistakes costs more time than typing a little slower. Numbers and punctuation are the most common slowdowns, so practise them in the dedicated modes until they feel automatic.
## Who should take a typing speed test?
Students, office workers, programmers, writers, gamers and data entry professionals all benefit from faster, more accurate typing. A quick typing speed test helps job seekers prove their WPM on a résumé and gives anyone who spends the day at a keyboard a simple goal to beat. ## Typing test FAQ
A typing test measures how fast and accurately you type. You type a passage of text while the test counts your words per minute (WPM), accuracy and errors.
The standard way: (correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes. Five characters count as one word, so longer words move the score more. Net WPM subtracts errors while raw WPM ignores them — both are shown after every round.
1 minute is the most popular length and is enough for a quick check. Longer tests (3, 5 or 10 minutes) give a more stable result because they average out short bursts of speed and fatigue.

## Keyboard Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-typing-test.html

Test your keyboard speed and accuracy. Works on any keyboard — laptop, mechanical or full-size. Instant WPM results, free, no sign up.

## Keyboard typing test
A keyboard typing test checks how fast you type on your keyboard and how accurate you are. It works the same on laptop, mechanical and full-size keyboards. Measuring regularly shows whether a new keyboard or layout actually improves your speed.
## Test any keyboard, not just the one you own
A keyboard test answers one question honestly: how fast are your hands on this keyboard? Laptop keyboards, mechanical switches and full-size boards all have different travel and feedback, and your WPM shifts with them. Test the keyboard you use for work, then test the one you game on; the difference tells you which one your hands actually like.
## Keyboard typing tips
Keep your wrists relaxed and fingers anchored on the home row. Use all ten fingers rather than hunting and pecking. A comfortable keyboard with good key travel helps, but consistent practice matters far more than the hardware.
## Works with any keyboard layout
This keyboard typing test runs on QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak and Colemak alike — it simply measures the characters you type against the target text. Membrane, mechanical or laptop scissor-switch, the physical board doesn't change the score. What matters is muscle memory: knowing where each key sits without looking so your hands stay anchored on the home row.
## Build true touch typing
Touch typing means typing without watching your fingers. Use the small bumps on the F and J keys to find the home row by feel, then return to it after every reach. The on-screen keyboard below highlights the next key so you can gradually stop looking down at your real keyboard and trust your hands instead.
## Typing test FAQ
Technique matters more than hardware, but a comfortable keyboard with good key travel can help you type faster and more accurately.

Yes — this test works on any keyboard, so it's great for comparing a new mechanical board against your old one.
Mechanical keyboards usually add 3 to 8 WPM from cleaner key feel and fewer missed presses, but the gap shrinks with practice. Test both here and keep the one whose accuracy stays higher after ten rounds, not just the faster-feeling one.

## Number Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/number-typing-test.html

Practise typing numbers fast and accurately. Numeric typing is a separate skill from text — essential for data entry, accounting and finance. This number typing test measures your digit speed and accuracy.

## Number typing test
The number typing test focuses on digits instead of words. Typing numbers quickly is a distinct skill: the top row and numeric keypad use different finger movements than regular text, and most people are far slower at numbers than letters. Regular practice closes that gap — vital for data entry, accounting, finance and spreadsheet work. In offices this same drill is called the ten key punch test or ten key test, named after the ten-key numeric pad. The keys and the muscle memory are identical, so scores carry across both names.
## How to type numbers faster
Use the numeric keypad on a full keyboard and anchor your fingers on the 4-5-6 home row. On a laptop, practise the top number row until you can hit digits without looking. Prioritise accuracy first — a mistyped number is often worse than a mistyped word — then build speed with daily reps.
## Number row versus numeric keypad
There are two ways to type numbers: the top number row and the dedicated numeric keypad on full-size keyboards. This test drills the number row, which every keyboard has — including laptops. Mastering it means you can enter dates, prices and codes mid-sentence without moving your hands away from the home row.
## Where fast number typing pays off
Accountants, data-entry clerks, developers and anyone working with spreadsheets type digits constantly. Clean, quick number entry cuts costly transposition errors — typing 1,243 instead of 1,423 — and speeds up any task built on figures. Regular practice turns the number row from a slow reach into automatic muscle memory.
## Typing test FAQ
It measures how fast and accurately you type digits (0-9) rather than words. Your speed is still reported in WPM, where every 5 characters counts as one word.
Numbers are typed less often than letters, and the top row or numeric keypad use different finger patterns. Most people type numbers 30-50% slower than text until they practise.
Yes, completely free, no sign up and no ads inside the typing area. Your results are saved only in your own browser.
You can use either the number row or the numeric keypad — whichever you want to practise. The test just checks the digits you type against the target.
Yes. A ten key punch test, ten key test and number typing test all measure how fast you key digits on the numeric pad. Some employers use the ten key name for their data entry screening, but the measurement — digits per minute and accuracy — is exactly what this page scores.

## Punctuation Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/punctuation-typing-test.html

Drill commas, periods, quotes and symbols with a punctuation typing test. Punctuation is where accuracy drops most, so train it directly and watch your WPM improve.

## Punctuation typing test
Punctuation marks sit on the hardest-to-reach keys and often need the Shift key, so they are the biggest source of typing errors. This punctuation typing test feeds you real sentences full of commas, full stops, apostrophes, quotes and brackets so you can practise them in context.
## Tips for accurate punctuation
Slow down slightly before a punctuation mark, keep your fingers anchored on the home row, and learn the exact reach for each symbol. Accuracy matters more than speed here, because a misplaced comma or bracket is costly to fix.
## Why punctuation is harder to type
Letters live on the home and middle rows, but commas, apostrophes, quotation marks and brackets force your fingers to the edges of the keyboard — often with the Shift key held down. That reach breaks your rhythm, which is exactly why dedicated punctuation practice pays off for anyone who writes emails, essays or code all day.
## Punctuation worth drilling
Focus on the marks you actually use: periods, commas, apostrophes in contractions, question marks, colons and parentheses. Practising sentences full of real punctuation trains the Shift-plus-symbol combinations until they feel automatic, so your writing flows without constant pauses to hunt for the right key.
## Frequently asked questions
It is a typing test that emphasises punctuation marks and symbols, letting you practise commas, periods, quotes, brackets and more in real sentences.
Punctuation keys are on the edges of the keyboard and many need the Shift key, so they break your home-row rhythm until you practise them.
Yes, completely free with no account; punctuation drill results stay on your device.
The apostrophe, comma and hyphen lead because they need a pinky stretch plus a rhythm break; brackets and quotes follow for programmers. Drill them in short bursts rather than full tests — ten focused minutes beats an hour of mixed typing.

## Typing Accuracy Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-accuracy-test.html

Measure your typing accuracy, not just speed. See your error count and precision alongside WPM. Free, no sign up.

## Typing accuracy test
A typing accuracy test shows what percentage of characters you type correctly, alongside your WPM and error count. Accuracy is often more valuable than raw speed — a fast typist who makes many mistakes is slower overall once corrections are counted.
## How to improve accuracy
Slow down slightly and aim for zero errors first; speed follows naturally once your fingers learn the correct movements. Focus on the keys you miss most, and keep your eyes on the screen so you can catch mistakes as they happen.
## Why accuracy beats raw speed
A blazing WPM means little if half your words need fixing. Every mistake costs a backspace and a retype, so real-world typing speed depends far more on accuracy than on peak pace. This test shows accuracy next to WPM and counts your errors, so you can see exactly where clean typing is quietly slowing you down.
## How to type more accurately
Start slower than feels natural and let correct keystrokes build muscle memory — rushing only teaches your fingers the wrong moves. Watch for your personal problem keys (often the top row and punctuation), keep a light, even rhythm, and resist the urge to glance at the keyboard. Aim to hold accuracy above 97% before you push for speed.
## Typing test FAQ
Aim for 95% or higher. Professional typists usually stay above 97% accuracy while maintaining good speed.
Every error needs correcting, which costs time. High accuracy means your effective speed is close to your raw speed.

## typing practice
Regular typing practice is the only reliable way to get faster. Ten to fifteen minutes a day beats one long session once a week, because your muscles learn the key positions through repetition. Use this page every day: pick a mode, type the text, then compare your result with yesterday. Try to keep accuracy above 95 percent at all times. ## A simple practice plan
Week one: two minute sentence tests, focus on accuracy. Week two: add quotes and numbers, keep the same two minutes. Week three: try five minute tests to build endurance. Week four: switch back to one minute and compare your WPM with week one. Most people gain 10 to 20 WPM in a month with this routine. ## When practice stops working
A plateau near 50 or 70 WPM usually means one bottleneck, not general slowness: check your slowest keys in the result panel after each round. Spend a week drilling only those keys in accuracy test rounds at 97%+ before chasing speed again. If accuracy is fine but speed stalls, your rhythm is uneven — try 2 minute tests at a metronome-steady pace instead of sprinting. Most plateaus break within two focused weeks.

## Typing Lessons
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-lessons.html

Free typing lessons for every level. Learn touch typing one step at a time: home row first, then every finger, then real speed. Each lesson is a timed practice you can repeat until it feels effortless. No sign up, learn at your own pace.

## typing lessons
Good typing lessons build speed the safe way: one habit at a time. Touch typing means typing without looking at the keyboard, and it is the single biggest speed upgrade most people can make. Instead of hunting for keys with two fingers, you train all ten fingers so each key has a fixed finger and muscle memory takes over. The result is faster, steadier typing that also frees your eyes for the screen.
## Start every lesson with the home row
Every typing lesson plan starts in the same place: the home row. Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ; with your thumbs on the space bar. Feel for the small bumps on F and J; they tell your index fingers where to land without looking. Practice typing words made only of home row letters until you never have to think about it, because every other key is reached from this position.
## A free four week typing lesson plan
Week one: home row only, short one minute lessons, accuracy over speed. Week two: add the top row and the shift keys for capitals, two minute lessons. Week three: cover the bottom row and the number row, then try the number text set. Week four: mix sentences, quotes and punctuation, and test your WPM against week one. Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough; most learners reach 40 to 60 WPM within a month of daily lessons.
## Typing lessons order: what to learn first
Lessons only work in the right order. Learning speed before home row is the most common way people stall.
1. Home row - asdf jkl; until you can find each key without looking.
2. Top and bottom rows - add one row at a time; accuracy first, speed later.
3. Capitals and punctuation - use the capital letter typing test and punctuation typing test.
4. Numbers - separate skill; the number typing test covers it.
5. Speed and endurance - only now use the 1 minute and 5 minute timed tests as training.
## Typing lessons FAQ
Most people reach a comfortable 40 to 60 WPM with 10 to 15 minutes of daily practice for three to four weeks. Reaching 80 WPM or more takes a few more months of regular use, but the daily time stays the same.

Hunt-and-peck means looking at the keys and pressing them with one or two fingers, which is slow and tiring. Touch typing uses all ten fingers from the home row without looking, so typing becomes faster, more accurate and far less effort.

## learn to type faster
Most people who want to learn to type faster are already typing every day, so the problem is not volume but method. Two things hold typists back: looking at the keyboard, and fixing mistakes. When you stop looking down, your speed jumps almost immediately, because your eyes stop lagging behind your fingers. When you chase accuracy instead of raw speed, you stop losing time to backspacing, and speed rises on its own.
## What slows most people down
Three areas cause almost all slow typing: numbers, punctuation, and the shift keys. Most learners are fluent with common words but freeze the moment a digit or a comma appears. Turn your weakness into a drill: spend a few minutes a day on the number and punctuation text sets until they feel as easy as sentences. Also check that you press shift with the opposite hand, never by stretching the same finger across the keyboard.
## A four week plan to type faster
Week one: one minute tests only, target 98 percent accuracy, ignore speed entirely. Week two: add two minute tests and switch to quotes to train capitals and punctuation. Week three: use the number set daily, and start tracking your average WPM across the week. Week four: push for speed on one minute tests and compare with week one. Most typists add 10 to 25 WPM in a month with ten to fifteen minutes of this training a day.

## Typing Tips
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-tips.html

Small typing tips compound into big speed. Below are the habits that actually move the needle: how to sit, where to put your fingers, and how to train accuracy so speed follows. Read one tip, then test it on the timed practice right here. Free, no sign up.

## typing tips
The best typing tips are the boring ones, because typing is pure muscle memory. Anything you repeat daily becomes automatic, and anything you shortcut becomes a habit you later have to unlearn. Pick two or three tips below and apply them for a week rather than reading all of them once. Small adjustments to hand position and attention add up faster than any speed-typing trick.
## Posture and hand position tips
Sit with your feet flat, your forearms roughly level, and the top of your screen at eye height so your neck stays relaxed. Curve your fingers slightly and rest them on the home row: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they let your index fingers find home without looking. Keep your wrists floating rather than pressed hard onto the desk.
## Accuracy tips that also build speed
Look at the text, never your hands. Press every key with the finger that owns it on the home row rather than the nearest finger, even when it feels slower at first. Type to the end of a word before you fix an error, instead of stopping mid-word. And slow down to the speed at which you make almost no mistakes; that is the speed your fingers actually learn, and it rises on its own.
## How to type faster and more accurately: a weekly routine
Speed follows accuracy, not the other way round. This is the routine that raises both without turning practice into a chore.
Day 1-2: form only. Run slow rounds at 95%+ accuracy. Ignore WPM entirely.
Day 3-4: steady rounds. Hold a pace you can repeat. Use a 2 minute typing test so the score is comparable.
Day 5: push one round. Accept lower accuracy to find your ceiling, then go back to form work.
Day 6: weak keys. Identify the two or three letters that cost you most and drill them with typing practice.
Day 7: rest. Progress in typing is consolidated between sessions.
Two things reliably hold people back: looking at the keyboard, and chasing WPM while accuracy is still below 95%. Fix the second one first, with how to type without looking and typing accuracy test.
## Typing tips FAQ
Keep your fingers on the home row and look only at the screen. Once your hands learn where the keys are, speed becomes a matter of practice instead of searching.
Cover your hands with a cloth or dim the room light for a few minutes a day, and use the on-screen keyboard to check positions. The bumps on F and J give your index fingers a landmark, so trust them and keep your eyes on the text.
Each key has a home-row finger that owns it. Index fingers cover the middle columns and stretch outward, middle and ring fingers take their own columns, and the pinkies handle the outer edges plus the shift and enter keys. Practice slowly at first so each key keeps its fixed finger.
Slow down until you make almost no errors, finish each word before correcting, and practice the number and punctuation sets, which cause most mistakes. Accuracy is a habit, not a limit, and it is what ultimately raises your speed.
Feet flat, back supported, shoulders relaxed, forearms roughly parallel to the floor, and the screen top at eye height. Your wrists should float over the keyboard rather than resting heavily on the desk, which keeps your fingers quick and pain-free.

## Words Per Minute Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/words-per-minute-test.html

Measure your words per minute (WPM) with a free online speed test. Type for one minute or choose 15 seconds up to 10 minutes and get your WPM and accuracy instantly.

## words per minute test
A words per minute test (WPM test) measures how many words you can type in one minute. The rule is simple: every five characters counts as one word, so longer words add more to your score. Take the test, type the text shown on screen, and your WPM, accuracy and error count are calculated live as you type.
In practice a typing words per minute test is the same measurement under a different name: you type for a fixed time, the test counts correct characters, and dividing that count by five and by the elapsed minutes gives your WPM. Nothing else changes the number, so any result you see here is directly comparable with other typing tests. The name changes with word order too — WPM typing test, typing test WPM and words per minute test all point at the same measurement, so whichever phrasing you searched for, this page scores it the same way.
## What is a good WPM score?
What counts as fast depends on context, but the bands below hold for most desk work. Around 40 WPM is typical, 60 WPM handles office and writing work comfortably, and 80+ WPM is genuinely fast — professionals land between 90 and 120. New typists should chase 95%+ accuracy first; speed follows on its own.
Level | Typing speed | What it unlocks
Average adult | 40-50 WPM | Everyday typing
Good (office standard) | 60-80 WPM | Most office and writing jobs
Fast (top ~10%) | 80-100 WPM | Transcription and coding pace
Advanced (top ~1%) | 100+ WPM | Professional typist territory
Compare yourself properly on the average typing speed benchmarks, broken down by age and profession.
## WPM vs CPM
CPM means characters per minute. Some sites show CPM instead of WPM. Because one word equals five characters, you can convert easily: WPM = CPM / 5. This test shows you both numbers on the result panel so you can compare with any other typing test.
Prefer characters per minute? Try the CPM typing test, where CPM = WPM &times; 5.
## Typing test FAQ
It converts everything you type into a WPM score using the 5-characters-per-word standard, alongside accuracy and error counts. This page runs the test at 60 seconds, the standard length employers quote.
WPM = (correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes elapsed. The industry standard treats every 5 characters as one word, so longer words count more. Raw WPM ignores errors, while net WPM subtracts them.
Sixty seconds is the accepted standard for a reportable score. Shorter sprints flatter you; longer tests (3 to 5 minutes) are steadier. Retake and average three rounds for a number you can quote.

## 3 Minute Typing Test

## 3 minute typing test
The 3 minute typing test hits a sweet spot: it averages out short bursts of speed without the fatigue of a long round, which is why many pre-employment typing screenings use a 3-5 minute window. Compare it with the 1 minute typing test and the 5 minute typing test to see how length changes your score.
## Why test for 3 minutes?
Three minutes filters out the noise of a single lucky sentence while staying short enough to take every day. It reveals whether you can hold speed and accuracy together, the real signal employers care about. Build that endurance with guided typing practice.
## What is a good 3 minute WPM?
Around 40 WPM is average for adults, 60+ is good, and 80+ is professional. Over 3 minutes accuracy matters as much as speed, so aim to finish with 95% or higher accuracy.
## Mistakes that lower your 3 minute score
The costliest error is opening at sprint pace: typists who blast the first thirty seconds usually fade below their 1 minute average by minute three. Second is glancing at the keyboard after every mistake, which breaks rhythm and adds hesitation errors. Third is chasing raw speed while accuracy slides under 95% — each error costs both the keystroke and the correction. Hold a pace about 5% under your one-minute speed, keep your eyes on the screen, and let accuracy carry the score.

## 10 Minute Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/10-minute-typing-test.html

Test true typing endurance with a full 10 minute typing test. Ten minutes measures how well you hold speed and accuracy over long sessions - the closest test to a real workday of writing or data entry.

## 10 minute typing test
The 10 minute typing test is the ultimate endurance check. Ten minutes exposes fatigue that short rounds hide: most typists slow 5-15% between minute one and minute ten, so your score here reflects what you can truly sustain. Warm up first with a 1 minute typing test or a 5 minute typing test.
## Who needs a 10 minute test?
Anyone whose work is long-form typing - transcriptionists, writers, coders, data entry clerks. If you will type for hours, a 10 minute result predicts your real-day speed better than any sprint. Build up to it with structured typing practice sessions.
## How to pace a 10 minute test
Start about 10% slower than your 1 minute speed and settle into a rhythm you can hold. Sit up, keep wrists neutral, and take micro-pauses at sentence breaks. Finishing strong matters more than an early burst that fades.
## Reading your 10 minute result
Your ten-minute score tells two stories: the headline WPM, and the fade between your fastest and slowest minutes. A drop under 10% means solid endurance; 10 to 20% is normal and shrinks with practice; more than 20% points to tension — usually raised shoulders or held breath — rather than weak fingers. Check whether errors cluster late in the round, which signals fatigue, or scatter throughout, which signals an accuracy habit; then train the weakness with focused typing practice sessions.
## Preparing for a 10 minute typing test
A 10 minute typing test is an endurance event, not a sprint. Almost everyone finishes 10-15% slower than their 1 minute speed, and that is expected rather than a failure.
Set posture first - feet flat, wrists neutral, elbows near 90 degrees. Discomfort at minute three becomes lost accuracy by minute seven.
Pace, do not sprint - open at roughly 90% of your comfortable speed and hold it. Sprinting the first minute reliably costs more than it gains.
Stop correcting every slip - for an endurance score, constant backtracking costs more WPM than the error itself.
Breathe and relax the shoulders - tension is the main cause of late-round slowdown.
## 10 minute typing test FAQ
Most people type 5-15% slower by the end of a 10 minute test as fatigue sets in. Pacing yourself and staying relaxed helps limit the drop.

## Chinese typing test
A Chinese typing test measures how fast and accurately you type Chinese text. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so every extra correct character raises your score. Typing complete Chinese sentences is the most realistic way to measure everyday Chinese typing speed.
## How to improve Chinese typing
Practise with real sentences rather than isolated characters, keep your fingers relaxed over the home row, and watch the screen instead of the keyboard. Because each Chinese character carries far more meaning than a single Latin letter, accuracy matters more than raw key speed; slow down first and let speed follow.
## Typing Chinese characters
Chinese is written without spaces between characters, so your fingers learn long sequences of keystrokes rather than short word patterns. Re-typing the same sentence a few times builds muscle memory for the most common characters — 的, 一, 是, 不, 了 — which make up a large share of everyday Chinese text.
## Practising Chinese typing
This Chinese typing test uses natural, everyday sentences, so you practise the real rhythm of Chinese writing: clauses separated by 、 and 。, numbers in full form, and the punctuation patterns you meet in articles, chat and email. Switch between sentences, quotes and words modes above to vary your drills.

## Hindi typing test
A Hindi typing test measures how fast and accurately you type Devanagari script. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word. Typing full Hindi sentences — with matras, conjunct consonants and the क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ clusters — is the most realistic way to measure everyday Hindi typing speed.
## How to improve Hindi typing
Practise with real sentences rather than isolated letters, keep your fingers on the home row, and look at the screen instead of the keyboard. Hindi adds matras above and below the consonants, so slow down at first to learn those key positions; accuracy first, then speed.
## Devanagari and typing speed
Devanagari is a syllabic script: most consonants carry an inherent अ vowel, and matras change that vowel. Typing real sentences trains the frequent conjuncts — क्ष, त्र, व्र, ज्ञ — and the matras ा ि ी ो ै that appear in almost every Hindi word.
## Practising Hindi typing
This Hindi typing test uses natural, everyday sentences, so you practise the real word patterns of Hindi — common endings like -ना, -कर and -है — together with the । full stop and the punctuation you meet in real Hindi writing. Timed Devanagari practice is also the format of most Indian typing exams.

## Arabic typing test
An Arabic typing test measures how fast and accurately you type Arabic script. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word. ## How to improve Arabic typing
Practise with real sentences rather than isolated letters, keep your fingers on the home row, and watch the screen instead of the keyboard. Arabic is typed right to left, so let your hands move with the text from right to left; slow down at first and let speed follow.
## Right-to-left typing
Arabic script runs right to left, and most letters connect to what follows them, changing shape by position. Typing real sentences trains the frequent letters — ا ل م و ي — and the word-final letter forms that appear in almost every Arabic sentence.

## touch typing test
A touch typing test measures how fast and how accurately you type without looking at the keys. Touch typing means all ten fingers work from the home row, and your eyes stay on the screen the whole time. This free test runs for 60 seconds, scores your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy live, and highlights every error so you can see exactly which keys still trip you up. Because the practice sentences are taken from real touch typing lessons, taking the test is itself a lesson.
## Why take a touch typing test every day
Muscle memory is built by frequency, not by marathon sessions. A daily 60 second touch typing test is enough to keep the home row fresh and to expose the two or three keys that always slow you down. Track your WPM across a week and you will see the pattern: accuracy climbs first, and speed follows a few days behind. When your accuracy passes 98 percent, you know the keyboard has finally moved into your fingers.
## How to use this touch typing practice
Start by resting your index fingers on the small bumps on F and J, with the other fingers curling onto the home row beside them. Type the sentence on screen without glancing down; if you must look, look only after the line is finished. Keep your wrists floating and your shoulders down. After the test, read the error report: those keys, not your fastest ones, are your next practice targets.

## Your first lesson in learning to type
Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they are the only map a beginner needs. Type words made from the home row only, slowly, and let each finger return home after every key. If you must look, look after the word, never in the middle of it. That is the entire first lesson, and everything after it is just practice.
## How long does it take to learn to type?
Most people own the home row in a week and reach a comfortable 40 to 60 words per minute in three to four weeks of daily practice. The mistake beginners make is chasing speed early; accuracy is the foundation and speed is the building that arrives later. End every session on your slowest, most careful line, and your hands will learn faster than you expect.

## The trainer's four week plan
Week one is diagnosis: run three drills a day and read the error report without trying to fix anything. Week two, drill your two weakest keys twice as often as the rest. Week three, run the full minute at a speed where you make no errors, and live there. Week four, chase your personal best once a day and log it. Five words per minute each week is the only target, because tendons keep their own pace.
## Why training beats practice
Practice is typing a lot; training is typing the right thing a lot. The difference is the log. When you record your WPM and accuracy side by side each day, a speed that costs accuracy shows up immediately as a bad trade, and the drill that fixed your weak keys shows up as a permanent step up. Your hands will plateau; the trainer's answer is variety and rest, not more effort.

## Why test typing in your own language
Most typing tests assume English, but a keyboard is not the same in every language. Chinese and Hindi use input methods that add a composition step between keystroke and character. Arabic reverses direction and changes letter shapes mid-word. Spanish adds accented vowels. Testing in the language you actually write in is the only way to measure the speed that matters to you.
## How to compare across languages
Run the same one minute test in each language on the same day, and write the five numbers down. Most people are fastest in their dominant language and ten to twenty percent slower in the others, and the gap shrinks fast with a few minutes of daily practice in the weaker languages. Re-run the same set next month and the comparison is honest, because the test itself never changed.

## Dvorak Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/dvorak-typing.html

Practice and measure your typing in Dvorak. The on screen keyboard below is already set to the Dvorak layout, with finger guidance mapped to Dvorak hand positions, so what you see matches what your system layout produces. ## dvorak typing
Most typing tests show a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless when you practice Dvorak typing: the label you need to find is not on the key you press. This test flips the on screen keyboard to the Dvorak layout, keeping the physical key positions of QWERTY and relabelling every key, so the hand you need to move matches the finger guide on screen exactly as a Dvorak user sees their own keyboard.
Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system: the test only draws the Dvorak keyboard on this page. Switch your operating system input to Dvorak, start typing, and the test scores you exactly as it would in QWERTY, because the measuring logic reads the characters your layout produces, not the keys.
## Why switch to Dvorak
August Dvorak designed the layout in the 1930s so the most common letters sit on the home row, which means less finger travel between rows for almost every English word. Typists who switch usually report less strain in long sessions, and many reach a higher comfortable speed once the new muscle memory settles, which takes roughly two to four weeks of daily practice.
The honest trade off: Dvorak helps most for people who type a lot of English prose. Shortcuts that assume QWERTY positions stay where they were physically, and shared or public keyboards are QWERTY by default, so most Dvorak users keep a fast way to switch back.
## How to practice Dvorak typing
Set your operating system layout to Dvorak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY text while looking at a Dvorak keyboard. Start with short sessions of two to five minutes, and resist the urge to look at your hands: the finger guides on this page exist exactly to replace that habit.
Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week; that drop is the switch cost, not a sign Dvorak is wrong for you. Track your WPM here each day and compare accuracy rather than raw speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it.
## Dvorak typing FAQ
No. The test only shows a Dvorak keyboard on this page; you switch your own operating system input to Dvorak in its keyboard or language settings. The test then scores what your layout produces.
No. The Dvorak keyboard is drawn by the page itself, the test runs entirely in your browser, and your results are stored only in this browser.
At first, yes, usually much lower. That is the cost of rebuilding muscle memory and it passes in a few weeks. Measure accuracy first; once accuracy is back to your normal level, speed follows.
Yes. The keyboard toolbar has a QWERTY and Dvorak switch and your choice is remembered in this browser, so the same page works for either layout.
The vowels A, O, E, U, I move to the middle row under the left hand, and common consonants like T, N, S and H move to the right hand. The full relabelling is drawn on the on screen keyboard above.
Evidence is mixed: most studies show a modest speed gain at the high end and clearer reductions in finger movement and strain. The main benefit people report is comfort in long typing sessions rather than a guaranteed speed jump.

## One Hand Typing
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/one-hand-typing.html

Learn and measure one hand typing on a normal keyboard. Whether you type with one hand because of an injury, a permanent condition, or simply a hand that is busy holding a coffee, the technique below lets you reach useful speeds without special hardware or chording software. Take the test with one hand and see where you are today.

## one hand typing
One hand typing on a standard QWERTY keyboard is a real, learnable skill. The idea is not to hunt and peck with one finger, but to assign each finger a fixed zone of the keyboard so your hand develops a repeatable map of where every letter lives. With practice, single hand typists reach 40 to 70 WPM, which is fast enough for almost all desk work.
You do not need a one handed keyboard or chord input software. The regular keyboard you already own is enough, because the technique is about hand position and practice, not hardware.
## Hand position for one hand typing
Put your four fingers on the home row of the side you use: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L semicolon. The thumb works the space bar. Each finger owns the keys in its column plus the row above and below, and the index finger stretches across the middle column to cover the keys on the far side.
The stretch is the hard part at first, especially the keys farthest from your little finger. Slow drills at first are normal; speed comes from accuracy, because a hand that returns to home row after every key does not need to look down.
## How fast can one hand typing get
Beginners hunting with one finger sit near 15 to 25 WPM. With proper finger zones and a few weeks of short daily sessions, 35 to 50 WPM is common. Experienced one hand typists who type all day reach 60 to 70 WPM and occasionally higher.
Measure honestly with the test on this page: run a one minute test with one hand only, and record your accuracy beside your WPM. Accuracy below 90 percent usually means you are reaching for speed before the map is settled, so slow down until accuracy rises and let speed follow.
## One hand typing FAQ
Yes. With fixed finger zones and practice, one hand typists commonly reach 40 to 60 WPM and experienced ones 70 WPM or more. The key is using all fingers of that hand, not one finger hunting.
No. The technique works on any standard QWERTY keyboard. Specialised hardware can help for some people, but it is not required to reach useful speeds.
Use the hand you have. The finger zone method works symmetrically for either side; the test here does not care which hand presses the keys.
Basic fluency in two to four weeks with fifteen to twenty minutes a day. Getting back to your two hand speed takes longer, but useful working speed arrives faster than most people expect.
The test is self paced and as short as 15 seconds, so you can use it within whatever your recovery allows. It is not medical advice; follow your clinician's guidance about how much to type while healing.
Results are saved in this browser automatically, so run a one minute test every few days and watch the history table for your WPM and accuracy trend.

Your typing history, your chosen settings and your high score are saved in your browser's localStorage, which lives on your device only. Clearing your browser data or using a private window removes all of it. Nothing of yours reaches a database, because there is no database.

Typing.Rerivo is a free typing speed test that runs entirely in your browser. No account, no paywall, no upload: pick a duration from 15 seconds to 10 minutes, type, and get your WPM, accuracy and consistency instantly.

## Why this site exists
Most typing tests on the web are heavy pages that ask you to sign up, show ads between every test, or hide your results behind an email wall. This one is built the opposite way: one fast page, one test, one result, and everything stored in your own browser so your history stays yours.
It started as a single page and grew by listening to what people actually searched for: timed variants from 15 seconds to 10 minutes, practice for punctuation and capital letters, number and symbol drills, a certificate you can print, a Dvorak keyboard that matches your layout, and one hand typing practice for people who type with a single hand.
## How the measurement works
WPM uses the industry standard of five characters per word, counted from correctly typed characters divided by elapsed minutes. Accuracy is the share of correct keystrokes, and raw WPM counts every keystroke including mistakes, so the gap between the two shows how much correcting you do. Consistency measures how stable your speed was across the whole test rather than just the peak.
The text you type never leaves your browser, and there is no server-side scoring because there is no need for one: JavaScript on this page does all of it.

## Average Typing Speed
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/average-typing-speed.html

The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. 45–60 WPM is good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. Test your own speed below, then compare it with the benchmarks.

## What is the average typing speed?
The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy - that is where most adults land without deliberate practice. A speed of 45–60 WPM is considered good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. The table below shows how typing speeds are usually classified.
Skill level | Speed (WPM) | What it means
Beginner | Under 30 WPM | Still learning; hunt-and-peck on many keys
Below average | 30-45 WPM | Functional but slow; typing takes conscious effort
Average | 40-50 WPM | Where most adults land without practice
Good / above average | 60-80 WPM | Comfortable; meets most office job requirements
Fast | 80-100 WPM | Top ~10% of typists
Advanced / elite | 100+ WPM | Top ~1%; only about 1% type over 100 WPM
## Average typing speed by age
Typing speed is shaped more by how long someone has typed daily than by age itself, but it does follow a rough curve: it climbs through the teens, peaks in the late teens to twenties, then eases slightly later in life. These are approximate averages.
Age group | Average WPM | Notes
Under 13 | 15-30 WPM | Still building muscle memory; wide variance
13-18 | 35-55 WPM | Heavy phone users are often slower than expected
18-30 | 50-65 WPM | Peak learning years; fastest improvement
30-45 | 45-60 WPM | Stable; reflects accumulated work habits
45-60 | 40-55 WPM | Slight drop in raw speed, often higher accuracy
60+ | 30-45 WPM | Motor slowdown; practice still helps
## Typing speed by profession
Different jobs demand very different typing speeds. Roles where typing is the job - data entry, transcription, legal and executive support - expect well above average, while general office work is fine around 40–55 WPM. Accuracy usually matters as much as raw speed.
Job / role | Typing speed expected | Typical accuracy
General office work | 40-55 WPM | 95%+
Customer support / chat | 50-65 WPM | 97%+
Administrative assistant | 50-70 WPM | 97%+
Data entry | 60-80 WPM | 98%+
Medical transcription | 65-75 WPM | 98%+
Executive assistant | 70-80 WPM | 98%+
Legal secretary / paralegal | 70-90 WPM | 99%+
Benchmarks compiled from occupational typing data published by Wonderlic and TypingTest.now (2025-2026). Actual requirements vary by employer, test length, text and keyboard.
Want your own number? Take the typing speed test, measure it in characters per minute, or see the speeds employers require for jobs.
## How to type faster than average
If you are below the speed you want, the fastest way up is touch typing: use all ten fingers from the home row (ASDF JKL;) without looking at the keyboard. Prioritise accuracy over speed, practise 10–15 minutes a day, and keep your wrists relaxed. Most people add 10–20 WPM within a few weeks of daily practice.

On a normal QWERTY keyboard the fastest typists reach 150+ WPM. The highest reliably recorded speeds belong to Barbara Blackburn, who sustained 212 WPM on a Dvorak keyboard (a Guinness record), and Stella Pajunas, timed at 216 WPM back in 1946. Court reporters exceed 225 WPM, but on a specialised stenotype machine using shorthand chords, not a standard keyboard. For context the average is about 40 WPM, and professional typists aim for 97%+ accuracy.
Typing speed is measured in words per minute (WPM), where one word equals five characters including spaces. Net WPM subtracts errors, so WPM = (correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes.

## CPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/cpm-typing-test.html

This CPM typing test measures your speed in characters per minute. CPM counts every correct keystroke, so because one word is five characters, CPM = WPM &times; 5. Type the passage below to see your live CPM, WPM and accuracy.

## What is CPM (characters per minute)?
CPM means characters per minute - the number of correct characters you type in one minute, counting letters, numbers, spaces and symbols. It is simply a finer-grained version of typing speed. Because a word is defined as five characters, CPM = WPM &times; 5. The table below converts between the two.
WPM | CPM (= WPM &times; 5) | Level
20 WPM | 100 CPM | Beginner
40 WPM | 200 CPM | Average adult
60 WPM | 300 CPM | Good / office standard
80 WPM | 400 CPM | Fast
100 WPM | 500 CPM | Top ~1%
## CPM vs WPM: which should you use?
WPM and CPM measure the same thing on different scales, so neither is more accurate. WPM is the standard for ordinary prose typing. CPM is more common for numeric and data-entry work done on the number keypad, where whole words do not apply.
This test shows both your live CPM and WPM. For prose, see the words per minute test; for digits, try the number typing test.
## What is a good CPM typing speed?
The average adult types about 200 CPM (40 WPM). A good CPM is 250–300 (50–60 WPM), and 400+ CPM (80 WPM) is fast. Numeric data-entry roles commonly require at least 165 CPM on the keypad with 95%+ accuracy. See the full average typing speed benchmarks for context.
## Typing test FAQ
CPM stands for characters per minute - the number of correct characters you type in one minute, counting letters, numbers, spaces and symbols. It is a finer-grained measure of typing speed than WPM.
Divide CPM by 5, because a word is defined as five characters. So 300 CPM equals 60 WPM and 200 CPM equals 40 WPM. To go the other way, WPM × 5 = CPM.

Numeric data entry is done on the number keypad where whole words do not apply, so speed is measured in characters (or keystrokes) per minute. Employers commonly ask for at least 165 CPM with 95%+ accuracy.
Neither is better - they measure the same thing on different scales (CPM = WPM × 5). WPM is the standard for prose typing; CPM is more common for numeric and data-entry work.

## How pre-employment typing tests work

## Typing Practice for Programmers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-practice-for-programmers.html

Programmers type a lot of symbols, brackets and camelCase &mdash; the exact characters most typing tests skip. Most developers type 50&ndash;70 WPM on prose, but what really matters is fluent symbols and a low error rate. Practise the way you code: paste your own code with custom text, or drill punctuation and numbers below.

## Why typing speed matters for programmers
A good typing speed for a programmer is 50-70 WPM, but coding is not a typing race - you spend far more time thinking than typing. Speed matters where it removes friction: the faster your fingers find brackets, operators and names, the less a thought is interrupted on its way to the screen. Accuracy matters even more, because a mistyped symbol is a syntax error you have to hunt down.
## What slows programmers down
Code is dense with characters that ordinary typing practice never covers - brackets, semicolons, operators, and numbers - plus naming styles like camelCase and snake_case that break your rhythm. The fix is to practise those specific characters, not more prose.
What you type in code | Why it is slow | Practise it here
Brackets & symbols () {} [] ; = > | Rare in word tests; awkward reaches for the pinkies | Punctuation test
Numbers & operators | Top row and keypad use different muscle memory | Number test
Your real code | camelCase, indentation and your stack&rsquo;s idioms | Custom text
## How to practise typing as a developer
Paste a real file you work in using custom text and type it for accuracy, not speed. Spend a few minutes on the punctuation and number drills so symbol reaches become automatic. Keep your fingers on the home row and let the weak pinkies own the bracket and semicolon keys. Ten focused minutes a day beats one long session.
## Typing test FAQ
Around 50–70 WPM is typical and plenty for most development work. Coding is thinking-heavy, so fluent symbols and high accuracy matter more than raw prose speed.

Yes. Touch typing frees your attention for the logic instead of the keyboard, and makes symbol-heavy code far less error-prone.

## How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-to-type-without-looking.html

To type without looking, rest your fingers on the home row &mdash; left hand on ASDF, right hand on JKL; &mdash; feel the small bumps on F and J, and let each finger own its own keys. The skill is called touch typing, and it comes from short daily practice, not talent. Here is exactly how to build it, then test yourself below.

## Start on the home row (ASDF JKL;)
Put your left index finger on F and your right index finger on J - both have a raised bump so you can find them without looking. Your other fingers fall onto A S D and K L ; . This is &lsquo;home&rsquo;: every key is reached from here and your fingers return here between keystrokes. Each finger is responsible for the keys directly above and below its home key.
## Train muscle memory, not your eyes
The whole skill is not looking down. Keep your eyes on the screen, use the on-screen keyboard and hand guide below to see the next key, and resist peeking even when it feels slow at first. Practise 10-15 minutes a day and prioritise accuracy over speed - speed is just accurate muscle memory repeated. The touch typing test and the on-screen keyboard test highlight the next key and the correct finger as you go.
## How long until you can touch type?
Most people stop needing to look within a few weeks of daily practice, and return to their old speed within one to two months - faster after that, because touch typing has no ceiling the way hunt-and-peck does. Check your progress against the average typing speed as you go.
## Typing test FAQ
Rest your fingers on the home row (ASDF for the left hand, JKL; for the right), find the bumps on F and J by feel, keep your eyes on the screen, and let each finger own its keys. Practise a little every day.
Most people stop peeking within a few weeks of short daily practice, then take another month or two to match their old hunt-and-peck speed. Cover the keys and trust the F and J bumps to go faster.
A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. F and J have raised bumps so you can locate the home row without looking.
Looking down breaks your focus on the text and caps your speed. Typing by feel keeps your eyes on the screen and lets muscle memory take over, which is faster and more accurate.
Yes. Touch typing is muscle memory, not talent or age — short, consistent daily practice works at any age.

## Colemak Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/colemak-typing.html

Practice and measure your typing in Colemak. The on-screen keyboard below is already set to the Colemak layout, with finger guidance mapped to Colemak hand positions, so what you see matches what your system layout produces. Use the QWERTY / Dvorak / Colemak switch in the keyboard toolbar any time. Switch your operating system to Colemak, take the test, and get WPM, accuracy and consistency.

## colemak typing test
Most typing tests only draw a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless for Colemak typing practice: the label you are hunting for is not on the key you press. This test flips the on-screen keyboard to the Colemak layout, keeping the physical QWERTY key positions and relabelling every key, so the finger guide on screen matches exactly what a Colemak typist sees.
Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system. The page only draws the Colemak keyboard; you switch your operating system input to Colemak, start typing, and the test scores the characters your layout produces - so your WPM, accuracy, consistency and the per-key heatmap are all measured for real Colemak typing.
## Why Colemak
Colemak was published in 2006 as a middle path between QWERTY and Dvorak. It keeps the common shortcut keys Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places and changes only 17 keys, so the switch is far gentler than Dvorak while still putting the most-used letters under your fingers.
On the same English passage, Colemak keeps about 73% of letters on the home row (QWERTY is near 36%) and cuts repeated same-finger presses to roughly 1.5%, versus about 7.9% on QWERTY. Less finger travel usually means more comfort over long sessions; it does not guarantee a higher top speed, which still depends mostly on practice.
## How to practice Colemak typing
Set your operating system input to Colemak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY characters while looking at a Colemak keyboard. Start with short two-to-five minute sessions and resist looking at your hands - the finger guide and on-screen keyboard exist to replace that habit.
Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week or two; that is the switch cost, not a verdict on Colemak. Track accuracy here before speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it. Compare Colemak with Dvorak and QWERTY on the keyboard layouts page.
## Colemak typing FAQ

No. The Colemak keyboard is drawn by the page itself, the test runs entirely in your browser, and your results are stored only in this browser.
For most QWERTY typists, yes. Colemak changes only 17 keys and keeps Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY positions, so common shortcuts and much of your muscle memory still apply. Dvorak moves almost every key.

Colemak keeps the bottom row's Z X C V B and the Q W A positions, and remaps the rest so E, T, N, S, I, R and O land on the home row. The full relabelling is drawn on the on-screen keyboard above.

## Keyboard Layouts Compared
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-layouts.html

QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and Workman compared on home-row use, finger travel and same-finger presses &mdash; so you can see which keyboard layout fits you before you commit weeks to switching. Try any of them on the test below with a layout-matched on-screen keyboard and finger guide.

## QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak vs Workman
A keyboard layout is just the map of which letter sits under each key. QWERTY has been the default since the 1870s, but alternative layouts rearrange the letters so the most common ones sit on the home row, cutting finger travel. Here is how the four best-known layouts compare on the same English text.
Layout | Introduced | Finger travel* | Home-row use | Same-finger
QWERTY | 1870s | 153 m (baseline) | 36% | 7.9%
Dvorak | 1936 | 88 m (&minus;42%) | 71% | 3.2%
Colemak | 2006 | 89 m (&minus;42%) | 73% | 1.5%
Workman | 2010 | 84 m (&minus;45%) | 67% | 2.0%
*Modeled finger travel for the same 5,847-character English passage on a standard keyboard, with the share of letters typed without leaving the home row and the share of consecutive keys pressed by the same finger. Figures from the Typing Cat layout comparison lab; they are estimates of movement, not measured typing speeds.
## Which keyboard layout is best?
There is no single best layout, because less finger movement is not the same as faster typing. QWERTY wins on familiarity: it is on every shared computer and every shortcut assumes it. Dvorak alternates hands the most (about 67% of keystrokes), which many typists find rhythmic for long English prose. Colemak keeps the most letters on the home row (73%) and the fewest awkward same-finger presses (1.5%) while leaving Z, X, C, V and most shortcuts in place, so it is the usual pick for QWERTY users who want to switch. Workman trims total finger travel the most by also minimising sideways stretches.
For almost everyone, practice and accuracy move your WPM far more than the layout does. A fast QWERTY typist will beat a beginner on any layout. Switch for comfort and reduced finger travel, not for a guaranteed speed jump.
## Should you switch keyboard layout?
Switching costs you one to four weeks of slower, deliberate typing while new muscle memory forms, and shared or public machines will still be QWERTY. The payoff is less finger travel and, for many people, more comfort in long sessions. It is worth it mainly if you type a lot of English every day and own the keyboards you use most.
If you want the gentlest change, start with Colemak because it keeps your common shortcuts. If you love hand-alternation, try Dvorak. The honest answer for casual typists is that staying on QWERTY and practising is the higher-return move.
## Try each keyboard layout here
You can practise two of these layouts right now with a matching on-screen keyboard and finger guide: take the Colemak typing test or the Dvorak typing test, or measure your current speed on QWERTY with the main typing speed test. Each shows WPM, accuracy, consistency and a per-key heatmap so you can compare how a layout feels for you.
## Keyboard layouts FAQ
No layout is reliably fastest for everyone. Modeling shows Dvorak, Colemak and Workman cut finger travel by roughly 42 to 45% versus QWERTY, but measured typing speed depends far more on practice and accuracy than on the layout. The world's fastest typists use several different layouts, including QWERTY.
Dvorak puts about 71% of letters on the home row versus QWERTY's 36% and alternates hands more, which many typists find more comfortable for long English text. Studies show modest speed gains at best, so the main benefit is reduced finger movement and comfort, not a guaranteed speed jump.
Colemak keeps more letters on the home row (about 73%) and the lowest same-finger rate (about 1.5%), and it changes only 17 keys while keeping Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places, so it is easier to switch to than Dvorak. Dvorak alternates hands more. Which feels better is personal.
Code uses far more punctuation, brackets and symbols than English prose, so prose-optimised layouts help less. Programmer variants such as Programmer Dvorak and Workman Programmer rearrange the number and symbol rows. Many developers stay on QWERTY because editors, shortcuts and pair-programming all assume it.
Most people reach usable speed again in one to four weeks of short daily practice, and return to their old speed over one to three months. Accuracy recovers before raw speed, so track accuracy first.
Yes. This site has a free Dvorak typing test and a free Colemak typing test, each with an on-screen keyboard relabelled to that layout and a matching finger guide, so you can practise and measure your WPM without installing anything.

## 10 Key Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ten-key-typing-test.html

A 10 key typing test measures how fast you type on the numeric keypad &mdash; the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard &mdash; using the fingers of your right hand. It is the standard speed test for data entry, accounting and finance work. Take the timed number-pad test below and get your speed instantly.

## What is a 10 key typing test?
10 key typing (also written ten key typing or 10-key) is touch typing on the numeric keypad: the number, arithmetic and Enter keys on the right of a full-size keyboard. Instead of hunting for digits across the top row, a 10 key typist keeps the right hand anchored on 4 5 6 with the index, middle and ring fingers, and reaches every other key from there. It is the skill behind fast data entry, bookkeeping and banking work.
This page runs a numpad typing test in numbers mode, so the practice text is digits, decimals, dates and amounts - exactly the characters a 10 key operator types all day. Switch the Time chips to 15 or 30 seconds for a quick check, or run 3-5 minutes for a stable result.
## The 10 key home row (4 5 6)
Rest your index finger on 4, your middle finger on 5 and your ring finger on 6 - these three usually have a raised bump or a dot so you can find them without looking. The index finger also covers 1 and 7, the middle covers 2 and 8, the ring covers 3 and 9, and the little finger handles 0, . and Enter. Your thumb rests on the 0 key on many layouts.
The golden rule of ten key typing is the same as touch typing on the letter keys: eyes on the screen, fingers always returning to 4 5 6 between digits. Speed comes from never looking down.
## How is 10 key speed measured?
10 key speed is usually quoted in keystrokes per hour (KPH) or characters per minute (CPM), not words per minute. A comfortable 10 key speed for data entry is about 8,000-10,000 KPH (roughly 130-165 CPM), and strong operators reach 12,000-15,000 KPH with 99%+ accuracy.
Level | 10 key speed
Beginner | 3,000-5,000 KPH
Average | 5,000-8,000 KPH
Data entry ready | 8,000-10,000 KPH
Fast / professional | 12,000-15,000+ KPH
This test reports your characters per minute live; multiply by 60 to get an approximate keystrokes-per-hour figure, or use the dedicated keystrokes per hour test.
## Why practise the number pad separately?
The top number row and the numeric keypad use completely different muscle memory. Typing letters fast does not make you fast at the number pad, and many people lose a data entry job interview on the 10 key portion alone. Practising the numpad on its own trains the right hand to hit 0-9 and the decimal point without a single glance at the keyboard.
If you need both, warm up with this 10 key typing test and then check your general speed on the number typing test or the main typing speed test.
## 10 key typing FAQ
A 10 key typing test measures how quickly you type on the numeric keypad (the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard) using your right hand, keeping the fingers anchored on the 4, 5 and 6 keys.
For data entry work, aim for at least 8,000 keystrokes per hour (about 133 characters per minute). Experienced operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy or better.
It is touch typing applied to the numeric keypad. You keep your eyes on the screen, rest the fingers on 4 5 6, and let each finger own its column of digits.
Practise a few minutes a day with your eyes off the keyboard, keep the index, middle and ring fingers on 4, 5 and 6, and prioritise accuracy - errors cost more time than a slightly slower but clean run.
On laptops with no dedicated keypad you can use an external USB numeric keypad, or practise the digits with the number-typing mode instead, which uses the top number row.
