## Keystrokes Per Hour Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keystrokes-per-hour-test.html

A keystrokes per hour (KPH) test measures typing speed the way many data entry employers do &mdash; in keystrokes over an hour, not words per minute. Data entry roles commonly require 8,000&ndash;10,000 KPH. Type the passage below and convert your result to KPH instantly.

## What is keystrokes per hour?
Keystrokes per hour (KPH or KSPH) counts how many individual key presses you make in an hour, counting every character including spaces. It is the standard measure for data entry and numeric keypad work because it does not depend on how long the words happen to be. A fast data entry operator reaches 10,000-15,000 KPH.
If you know your characters per minute (CPM), multiply by 60 to get KPH: a steady 160 CPM equals 9,600 KPH. This test shows your characters per minute live, so you can read your KPH straight off the result.
## KPH vs WPM vs CPM
All three describe the same typing, just at different scales. WPM counts words (5 characters each) per minute; CPM counts characters per minute; KPH counts keystrokes per hour. Because a &lsquo;word&rsquo; is standardised as 5 characters, the conversions are fixed:
Your speed | WPM | CPM | KPH
Average | 40 | 200 | 12,000
Good | 60 | 300 | 18,000
Fast | 80 | 400 | 24,000
Elite | 100 | 500 | 30,000
The table assumes no error penalty; employers usually apply a net-accuracy penalty, so your effective KPH is lower than the raw figure.
## What KPH do data entry jobs require?
Job postings for data entry and clerical work often ask for 8,000-10,000 KPH with a high accuracy rate; some set the bar at 12,000 KPH. Numeric roles may test the number pad specifically, so pair this test with the 10 key typing test. Measure your text speed here and your WPM on the words per minute test, then check the requirements in the typing test for jobs page.
## Keystrokes per hour FAQ
For data entry work, 8,000 to 10,000 KPH is the usual requirement, and fast operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy. General office roles often accept lower KPH because typing is only part of the job.
WPM = KPH ÷ 300. Because 1 word is 5 characters and there are 60 minutes in an hour, 60 WPM equals 18,000 KPH.
Multiply characters per minute by 60: 160 CPM equals 9,600 KPH.

## Typing Speed Calculator
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-calculator.html

This typing speed calculator tells you how your typing speed converts between WPM (words per minute), CPM (characters per minute) and KPH (keystrokes per hour). Measure your real speed with the test below, then use the formulas and table to convert any figure. Everything runs in your browser.

## How to calculate typing speed (WPM)
Typing speed in words per minute (WPM) is worked out with one simple formula: WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes. Every five characters count as one &lsquo;word&rsquo;, so longer words are worth more. Net WPM subtracts your errors first: net WPM = ((correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes). Employers use net WPM, because a mistake you have to fix costs time.
To get your own numbers, just take the timed test above - it computes WPM, raw WPM, CPM and accuracy for you, so you can read your result straight off the scoreboard.
## WPM, CPM and KPH conversions
The three common typing-speed units are all fixed multiples of each other, so you can convert any of them by hand:
From | To | Formula
CPM | WPM | WPM = CPM ÷ 5
WPM | CPM | CPM = WPM × 5
CPM | KPH | KPH = CPM × 60
WPM | KPH | KPH = WPM × 300
WPM | | WPM = (characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes
So 60 WPM = 300 CPM = 18,000 KPH. These are the standard conversions used by typing certificates and data entry employers.
## Worked examples
If you type 300 characters in 1 minute, that is 300 ÷ 5 = 60 WPM (or 18,000 KPH). If you type 1,200 characters in 3 minutes, that is (1,200 ÷ 5) ÷ 3 = 80 WPM. If you make 12 mistakes over that run, your net speed is (1,200 &minus; 12) ÷ 5 ÷ 3 = 79 WPM.
Want the measured number instead of the maths? Run the words per minute test for WPM, the CPM typing test for characters per minute, or the keystrokes per hour test for KPH.
## Typing speed calculator FAQ
WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes elapsed. Every 5 characters count as one word, so 300 characters in 1 minute is 60 WPM.
Divide characters per minute by 5. So 250 CPM is 50 WPM, and 400 CPM is 80 WPM.
Multiply WPM by 300. For example, 60 WPM equals 18,000 keystrokes per hour.
Gross WPM counts every character you typed; net WPM subtracts your errors first. Employers almost always use net WPM because it reflects usable output.
Yes. The typing speed calculator and every typing test on this site are completely free, with no sign-up and no account.

## Quick Brown Fox Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/quick-brown-fox-typing-test.html

The &lsquo;the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; sentence is the most famous pangram in typing practice &mdash; a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. Typing it is the traditional warm-up and a quick way to check that every key on your keyboard works. Take the test below and measure your speed and accuracy.

## What is the quick brown fox sentence?
&lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; is a pangram: a sentence that uses all 26 letters of the alphabet at least once. Because it covers the whole keyboard it has been the standard typing drill for over a century, and it is still used to test typewriters, keyboards and fonts. Practising it warms up every finger before a longer typing test.
Type it a few times here - the test scrolls through alphabet-rich sentences in the same spirit, so your warm-up trains every letter rather than only the common ones.
## Why practise with pangrams?
Ordinary sentences repeat the same handful of common letters and rarely touch q, z, x or j. A pangram forces every key into the run, which is exactly what you need before a speed attempt: it surfaces the awkward keys while the stakes are low. That is why &lsquo;quick brown fox&rsquo; games appear in almost every typing tutor and school typing class.
For a targeted version, the keyboard typing test highlights the next key and the correct finger, and the easy typing test uses simple high-frequency words if the pangram still feels hard.
## Quick brown fox and keyboard checking
Because the pangram contains every letter, typing it is the fastest way to confirm that no key is broken or stuck: if a letter is missing from the output, that key is faulty. Try it with capitals and punctuation too - &lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.&rsquo; - to exercise the shift keys and the full stop. Then move on to a full typing speed test to get your WPM.
## Quick brown fox FAQ
&lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; is a pangram - a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. It has been the classic typing-practice sentence for over a century.
Because it uses all 26 letters, it exercises every key and finger in one short line, making it an ideal warm-up and a fast way to check that your keyboard works.
It is a good warm-up, but the unusual letters (q, z, x) make it harder than common-word practice. Beginners may prefer the easy typing test first.
The classic sentence is nine words: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. It contains 35 letters.
Yes. If a letter is missing from what you type, that key is faulty. Include the full stop and capitals to test shift and punctuation keys as well.

## Home Row Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/home-row-typing-test.html

The home row is the row of keys your fingers rest on &mdash; A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right. Every key on the keyboard is reached from here, which is why home-row practice is the first lesson in touch typing. Take the timed test below to drill the home row and track your progress.

## What is the home row?
The home row (also called the home keys) is the middle row of the keyboard where your fingers rest between keystrokes: A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right hand. The F and J keys have small raised bumps so your index fingers can find home by feel alone, without looking down.
Home-row typing is the foundation of touch typing. Each finger owns a column of keys and always returns to its home key, so the hand never has to hunt for a letter. Start by typing only home-row letters until they feel automatic, then add the rows above and below.
## Which finger types which home key?
Home key | Finger | Also reaches
A | Left pinky | Q, Z, 1
S | Left ring | W, X, 2
D | Left middle | E, C, 3
F | Left index | R, T, G, V, B, 4, 5
J | Right index | Y, U, H, N, M, 6, 7
K | Right middle | I, comma, 8
L | Right ring | O, full stop, 9
; | Right pinky | P, slash, 0
The thumbs rest on the space bar. Keeping this assignment is what lets you type without looking - see the full method on how to type without looking.
## Home row drills and practice
Effective home-row practice repeats the eight home keys in short, varied bursts rather than long paragraphs, so your fingers build the exact movements they need. Run this test for 1 or 2 minutes a day, aiming first for perfect accuracy and only then for speed. When the home row feels natural, move on to the touch typing test and the keyboard typing test, which introduce the surrounding rows with an on-screen finger guide.
## Home row FAQ
A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right hand, with the thumbs on the space bar. F and J have raised bumps so you can find the row without looking.
It is the base position of touch typing. Every key is reached from home and the fingers return there, so you never have to look down to find a letter.
Left hand: pinky on A, ring on S, middle on D, index on F. Right hand: index on J, middle on K, ring on L, pinky on ;.
Most people feel comfortable within a few days of short daily practice, but full touch typing across all rows takes a few weeks of consistent practice.
No. Keep your eyes on the screen and use the F and J bumps to find home. Looking down slows the muscle memory you are trying to build.

## You can still learn to type faster as an adult
It is a common myth that only children can build typing speed. ## Typing Skill Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-skill-test.html

A typing skill test tells you how good you are at typing: your words per minute (WPM), your accuracy and your error rate, combined into one clear picture of your typing skill level. It is the same kind of test used for job applications and typing exams. Take it below and get your score instantly.

## What is a typing skill test?
A typing skill test (also called a typing skills test or typing proficiency test) measures how fast and how accurately you can type a passage. You are timed, and your result is reported as WPM plus an accuracy percentage and an error count. Employers, schools and government exams use this format to compare candidates objectively.
Unlike a plain speed test, a skill test is judged on the combination of speed and accuracy. 70 WPM at 90% accuracy is a weaker result than 60 WPM at 99%, because the errors have to be fixed and cost real time.
## What counts as a good typing skill score?
Skill level | WPM | Accuracy
Beginner | under 30 | under 90%
Basic | 30-40 | 90-95%
Proficient | 40-60 | 95-98%
Advanced | 60-80 | 98-99%
Expert | 80+ | 99%+
For most office jobs, 50-60 WPM with 97%+ accuracy is expected. For data entry, exams and specialised roles the bar is higher - see the typing test for jobs requirements.
## How to improve your typing skill score
Improvement comes from accuracy first, speed second. Slow down until you can type a full minute without errors, keep the fingers on the home row, and look at the screen rather than the keyboard. Practise daily for ten to fifteen minutes, mixing a general typing practice run with a targeted accuracy test. Boost weak spots with the weak-key drill, and check your standing against the average typing speed.

## Paragraph Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/paragraph-typing-test.html

Practise with full paragraphs instead of single words — the format real typing exams and job tests use.

## Paragraph vs word typing test
A word test flashes a list of common words, which rewards pure finger speed. A paragraph typing test gives you connected sentences with spaces, capitals and punctuation — closer to what you actually type at work, and to what most exams and employers set.
## Why paragraphs are harder
Paragraphs make you hold rhythm across long familiar phrases, returning to the home row for capitals and reaching for the comma and full stop without breaking flow. Because the text is real language, you also cannot autopilot a short list of repeated words — you have to read ahead.
## Choose your passage length
Use the timer chips to sit a 1-minute paragraph for a quick check, a 5-minute paragraph for practice, or a 10-minute paragraph for full exam stamina. Longer passages expose the speed decay that short bursts hide.
## How to use this page
Start typing and keep going until the timer runs out. Your WPM, accuracy and a per-second speed chart appear straight away. Practise two or three passages a day and review where your accuracy drops — that is where the lost words per minute hide.
## Paragraph Typing Test FAQ
It is a typing test where you copy a full passage of connected sentences rather than a list of single words, so capitals, spaces and punctuation count just as they do in real writing.
Exam passages are usually 300 to 500 words. On this page you choose 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 minutes so you can practise the exact length your exam or employer uses.
Yes. Real sentences add capitals, punctuation and reading ahead, so scores are typically a little lower than a pure word-list test — but far closer to your true working speed.

## Beginner Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/beginner-typing-test.html

New to typing? Start here: an easy, forgiving test that measures where you are today so you can watch yourself improve.

## A friendly first test
Most typing tests throw long words and heavy punctuation at you from the first keystroke. This beginner version keeps the text short and the words common, so you can finish a passage and actually see a score instead of drowning in errors.
## Where should a beginner start?
Begin with the home row — A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. Learn to reach each key with the correct finger instead of hunting with two fingers, even if it feels slower for the first few days. Speed is a by-product of accuracy; accuracy is a by-product of good technique.
## Don't chase speed yet
Aim for accuracy above 95% before you worry about words per minute. A beginner who types 25 WPM at 98% accuracy will outpace someone who types 40 WPM at 85% once corrections and real work are counted.
## Your first realistic targets
Most complete beginners sit around 20 to 30 WPM. Getting to 40 WPM is a realistic first goal within a few weeks of ten minutes a day. Kids and occasional typists may take longer; there is no rush and no score to beat but your own.
## Beginner Typing Test FAQ
Between 20 and 30 words per minute is normal for a beginner. Reaching 40 WPM within a few weeks of daily practice is a realistic first goal.
Accuracy. Aim for 95% or higher before pushing for speed — clean typing is faster in the long run because you spend less time fixing mistakes.
With about ten minutes a day, most beginners reach a comfortable 40 WPM in four to eight weeks. Touch typing properly takes a bit longer but pays off for life.
Yes — free, no sign-up, and your results stay in your browser.

## Timed Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/timed-typing-test.html

A ticking clock is the fairest way to measure typing speed. Choose your length and see how many words you can type before the buzzer.

## How a timed typing test works
You type for a fixed number of seconds or minutes and the test counts every correctly typed character, then converts it to words per minute. Because the clock never pauses for backspacing, a timed test rewards clean, steady typing over burst speed.
## Pick the right duration
Careers and most online tests use one minute, so a 1-minute timed test is the standard benchmark. Data-entry and government exams often run three or five minutes to test stamina. Sprint-style challenges use 15 or 30 seconds, and typing-race communities favour 10 minutes to expose who holds speed under fatigue.
## Why timing matters
Without a clock it is easy to slow down on hard words or rest on your laurels. A timer forces an even rhythm and gives you a number you can compare week to week — the only way to know whether your practice is actually working.
## Beat your own clock
Start shorter than you think you need: a 30-second timed test you finish cleanly teaches more than a 10-minute slog full of errors. Once you hold your accuracy above 97%, extend the duration and watch net speed stay flat — that is real progress.
## Timed Typing Test FAQ
A typing test where you type against a countdown clock for a set duration — usually 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 minutes — and your speed is measured in words per minute.
One minute is the most common, used by most online tests and employers. Career exams and government tests often use three to five minutes.
No. The clock keeps running so the score reflects your true working speed, including any slowdown caused by corrections.
Yes — use the duration chips to pick anything from 15 seconds to 10 minutes.

## Fast Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/fast-typing-test.html

Already comfortable on the keyboard? Measure just how fast you really are — and find the ceiling you can push past.

## What counts as fast typing?
The average person types around 40 words per minute. Above 60 WPM you are quicker than most people you will meet, and 80 WPM or more puts you in the top few percent of typists. Professional transcriptionists and programmers often sit between 80 and 120 WPM.
## Why some people type faster
Fast typists are not just fast — they are accurate. They touch type all ten fingers on the home row, keep their hands anchored, and read a few words ahead so their eyes never stall on a hard word. Raw finger speed matters far less than never breaking rhythm.
## Push past your plateau
Once you are fast, big gains come from fixing the few keys that cost you time. Turn on the on-screen keyboard highlight and notice which letters make you hesitate — then drill those. A single problem key fixed can add several words per minute.
## Test under pressure
A fast typing test is also a pressure test. Type for one minute at maximum effort, then look at the accuracy figure: if it dropped below 90%, you are typing beyond your control and would score higher by easing off slightly.
## Fast Typing Test FAQ
Anything above 60 words per minute is fast for a general typist. 80 WPM or more is top-tier, and professional typists often reach 100 to 120 WPM.
The all-time English record is above 200 words per minute, but that is a specialised achievement. For everyday users, 80 to 100 WPM already puts you in the top 1%.
Touch type with all ten fingers, keep accuracy above 97%, and drill the specific keys that make you hesitate. Speed follows clean technique, not rushing.
Yes, free and no sign-up.

## Hard Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/hard-typing-test.html

Easy text hides weak fingers. This hard test adds capitals, symbols and numbers so every part of the keyboard gets a workout.

## Why the text is harder
Real documents are not lists of clean short words. They contain capital letters, commas, apostrophes, dashes, numbers and long multi-syllable words. This hard test mixes all of them so you practise the reaches that a simple word test never touches.
## What a hard test exposes
A sudden shift to a capital sends your hand away from the home row; a number row stretch breaks your rhythm; heavy punctuation makes you hunt for a key you rarely use. Those are exactly the moments where speed and accuracy leak away in real work.
## How to score well on hard text
Slow your overall rate just enough to keep accuracy high, and use the correct fingers even for the awkward keys — the number row and both little fingers are the usual weak spots. Practising hard text on purpose is how easy text becomes effortless.
## When to step up to hard mode
If you already hold 90%+ accuracy on normal passages and want to keep improving, hard mixed text is your next challenge. Expect your WPM to dip at first; that is the point — you are training new reaches, and speed returns higher.
## Hard Typing Test FAQ
Difficult tests include capital letters, numbers, symbols, uncommon words and punctuation, forcing reaches far from the home row instead of simple repeated words.
Because your hand has to leave the home row for capitals and the number row, and unusual words slow your reading ahead. A lower score on hard text is normal.
Yes, if you already type normal text accurately. Hard passages train the reaches that ordinary practice ignores, which raises your ceiling.
Yes, free and with no sign-up.

## Advanced Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/advanced-typing-test.html

For people who already type well: a demanding passage and honest scoring to see whether you belong in the top percentile.

## Built for experienced typists
If you already clear 60 WPM comfortably, an easy test tells you nothing. This advanced test uses longer, richer passages and expects full command of capitals, punctuation and the number row — a genuine stretch for a practised touch typist.
## Targets for advanced typists
Professional transcriptionists, programmers and typists working from dictation live between 80 and 120 WPM. An advanced target is 80 WPM or more at 98% accuracy; anything above 100 WPM is elite and rare.
## Where advanced speed is really won
At this level you are not limited by finger speed but by attention: reading far ahead, holding rhythm through difficult phrases, and never looking at your hands. Small reductions in hesitation, not faster fingers, are what move an advanced score upward.
## Use it as a true benchmark
Take this test monthly and record your net WPM. Because the passages are demanding and consistent, a rising score here is a far better signal of genuine progress than a lucky 10-second sprint.
## Advanced Typing Test FAQ
Around 80 words per minute with 98% accuracy or better is advanced. Above 100 WPM is elite; professional transcriptionists and programmers often sit in the 80 to 120 WPM range.
The passages are longer and richer in capitals, punctuation and vocabulary, with number-row reaches, so it demands real technique rather than fast fingers alone.
Once a month is enough. Advanced skill changes slowly, and a monthly net-WPM reading gives a stable, meaningful benchmark.

## How Fast Can I Type?
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-fast-can-i-type.html

One minute is all it takes to answer the question. Type the passage and get your words per minute and accuracy instantly.

## Find your words per minute
Words per minute, or WPM, is the standard measure of typing speed. It is calculated from the number of correctly typed characters divided by five — the average length of an English word — over the time you typed. This page gives you a clean one-minute reading.
## How you compare
The average adult types around 40 WPM. Under 30 WPM is below average, 40 to 60 WPM is exactly average to comfortable, 60 to 80 WPM is fast, and above 100 WPM is rare and professional-level. These figures are for typing on a keyboard in your own language.
## What your score really means
Speed without accuracy is misleading. A 70 WPM score at 88% accuracy is worth less than 55 WPM at 99%, because in real typing you have to fix every error. Always read the two numbers together.
## Can you type faster?
Almost certainly yes. Almost everyone can gain ten to twenty words per minute by learning to touch type with all ten fingers and by drilling the specific keys that make them hesitate. Ten focused minutes a day is enough.
## How Fast Can I Type FAQ
The average adult types about 40 words per minute. Anything above 60 WPM is considered fast and 80 WPM or more is top-tier.
In words per minute, where one word equals five typed characters. Your WPM is the correct characters divided by five, per minute.
Take the one-minute test on this page — it gives you your exact words-per-minute score plus an accuracy percentage in sixty seconds.
Yes: learn to touch type with all ten fingers, keep accuracy above 97%, and practise deliberately for about ten minutes a day. Most people can add 10 to 20 WPM.

## Typing Test for Interview
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-interview.html

Employers often ask you to sit a typing test before or during an interview. Rehearse the exact format here so there are no surprises on the day.

## Why employers test typing at interviews
A typing test gives a fast, objective reading of a candidate's real ability. Rather than trusting a CV claim, recruiters sit you at a keyboard, start a clock and watch the score — usually one to three minutes of ordinary business text with capitals and punctuation.
## What employers expect
Admin, customer-service and support roles typically ask for 40 to 55 WPM with 95% or higher accuracy. Data-entry and transcription roles push to 60 to 70 WPM, or measure keystrokes per hour for numeric work. Government and legal positions often add a formal minimum that you must clear to qualify at all.
## Rehearse the real thing
Use the timer to simulate the exact length your employer uses, and type business-style passages rather than clean word lists. Practise proofreading on the fly: many tests mark you down for uncorrected errors, so type a little slower and cleaner than you can.
## Turn nerves into an advantage
Interview pressure costs most candidates five to ten WPM. Because you have practised the format here, the test itself will feel routine — that calm alone is often worth several words per minute.
## Interview Typing Test FAQ
Many do, especially for administrative, data-entry, customer-service and secretarial roles. It is usually a short timed test of one to three minutes.
Most administrative roles ask for 40 to 55 WPM with 95%+ accuracy. Data-entry and transcription roles often want 60 to 70 WPM.
Practise timed one to three-minute tests on business-style passages, keep accuracy above 95%, and rehearse typing cleanly under mild pressure.
Yes, free with no sign-up, so you can practise as often as you like.

## Bank Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/bank-typing-test.html

Banking and clerical exams often include a typing round with a strict accuracy cut-off. Practise the format and the pace here.

## Typing in banking exams
Many bank clerk and clerical recruitment exams include a typing test as a qualifying round: you must reach a set speed and accuracy, and failing it can end your application regardless of your written score. The format is a timed passage, usually in the language you applied in, with accuracy checked closely.
## The usual standard
Common requirements sit around 30 to 40 words per minute with at least 90% accuracy, and many boards set a hard floor on errors — a fixed number of mistakes is allowed and no more. Because the pass mark is about accuracy, clean typing beats raw speed.
## Passages and language
Bank typing rounds use ordinary prose, not technical jargon, but they are timed strictly and often use a fixed paragraph you cannot choose. Practise on uninterrupted passages of a few hundred words and get used to holding focus without fixing every tiny slip.
## How to practise
Set the timer to match your exam — often five minutes — and aim to finish comfortably under the error limit before you try to raise speed. Once you can pass at 97% accuracy, push your WPM up in small steps. Watch our data entry and government typing pages for the same family of clerical tests.
## Bank Typing Test FAQ
It is a timed typing round used in many bank clerk and clerical recruitment exams, where you must reach a minimum speed and accuracy to qualify.
Requirements vary by board, but most ask for around 30 to 40 words per minute with 90% or higher accuracy, often with a hard limit on allowed errors.
Accuracy. Banking typing rounds usually fail candidates who exceed the error limit, so a clean, correct passage matters more than a fast one.
Yes — use the timed test on this page with a five-minute setting to mirror a typical exam round.

## SSC Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ssc-typing-test.html

SSC typing rounds are a qualifying stage with a strict speed and accuracy bar. Practise the format here before the real thing.

## What the SSC typing test is
Several SSC recruitment exams include a typing test as a qualifying round, typically typing a passage in a set time to prove a minimum speed and accuracy. It is often held at a test centre and must be cleared to be considered for the post, no matter how well you did in the written exam.
## The usual requirement
SSC typing rounds commonly ask for around 35 words per minute in English, or roughly 30 words per minute in Hindi, with high accuracy. Some exams set the bar in a mix of speed and error count, so you must meet both to pass.
## Training for the format
The passage is delivered on screen and the clock does not stop, so the goal is steady, error-free typing rather than bursts of speed. Practise with light punctuation and everyday vocabulary — the passages are ordinary prose rather than technical text.
## Reaching the pass mark
Build your baseline with short daily sessions until you clear the required speed at 95%+ accuracy, then add a minute at a time to build stamina. Our government and bank typing pages cover the same clerical-test family; use them together for a rounded practice routine.
## SSC Typing Test FAQ
Yes. Several SSC exams include a qualifying typing round where you must reach a minimum typing speed and accuracy, usually tested at a centre.
Requirements vary by post and year, but roughly 35 words per minute in English or about 30 in Hindi is the commonly cited benchmark, with high accuracy.
Practise timed passages daily, keep accuracy above 95%, and build stamina for the full test length. Use a five-minute timer to mirror exam conditions.
Yes, free and no sign-up.

## Typing Test for Teachers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-teachers.html

Teachers type constantly — lesson plans, reports, marking, emails. See where your speed sits against what the job demands.

## Why typing matters for teachers
Teaching involves a constant stream of typed work: lesson plans, schemes of work, reports, feedback and parent emails. Being a comfortable typist saves hours every week and leaves more energy for the classroom.
## What speed is expected
Teaching itself rarely sets a formal typing test, but the admin side rewards 45 WPM or more with good accuracy. Office-based education roles and school administrators often expect the same 40 to 55 WPM range as other admin jobs, and support-staff interviews may include a short timed test.
## Tools teachers use
Mark and feedback, online portals and shared documents all reward fast, accurate typing. Keeping accuracy high means fewer corrections in reports that others will read, which matters as much as speed.
## Practise in small gaps
You do not need a big block of time. A one-minute test between lessons, repeated daily, is enough to lift your speed steadily. Watch the accuracy figure and aim to hold it above 96% as your WPM rises.
## Typing Test for Teachers FAQ
Usually not to teach, but office-based education roles and support-staff interviews may include a short timed typing test like other administrative jobs.
Around 45 words per minute or more with good accuracy is comfortable for the heavy admin load of teaching. Administrative roles often expect 40 to 55 WPM.
Use short one-minute tests in spare moments during the day. Daily short sessions raise speed faster than occasional long ones.
Yes, free with no sign-up.

## Keyboard Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-practice.html

Before speed comes familiarity. Practise finding every key without looking and build the habits that make fast typing possible.

## Start with the home row
Rest your left fingers on A, S, D, F and your right on J, K, L, ; — the home row. The F and J keys have small raised bumps so you can find them by touch. Every finger owns a column of keys and returns to the home row after each reach; that is the whole secret of touch typing.
## Practise, don't hunt
Hunting for keys with two fingers feels fast at first but caps your speed hard. Practising the correct finger for each key, even when it is slower to begin with, builds the muscle memory that makes fast typing automatic later.
## Use the on-screen keyboard
Turn on the virtual keyboard and the next-key highlight so you can see which finger should reach which key. The on-screen hand guide shows the correct finger for the letter you are about to type — follow it closely for the first few sessions.
## Little and often
Ten focused minutes a day beats one long weekly session. Keep accuracy above 97% and let speed rise on its own; rushing before the habits are set just trains mistakes. Return to this page whenever you want a clean, distraction-free practice space.
## Keyboard Practice FAQ
Start on the home row, use the correct finger for every key, and keep your eyes on the screen. Practise about ten focused minutes a day with instant feedback.
The home row is the middle letter row: A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. F and J have raised bumps to guide your fingers.
No. Looking at the keyboard stops you building muscle memory. Use the on-screen keyboard and hand guide instead, and trust your fingers to learn.
Yes, free and no sign-up, on desktop and mobile.

## Japanese Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/japanese-typing-test.html

Test your Japanese typing speed with real Japanese sentences mixing kanji, hiragana and katakana. Instant speed and accuracy results. Free, no sign up.

## Japanese typing test
A Japanese typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Japanese text — sentences that mix kanji, hiragana and katakana exactly the way everyday Japanese is written. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so the score stays comparable with the classic 1 minute typing test.
## Romaji input, kana input and the IME
Most people type Japanese with a romaji-to-kana IME: you type roman letters, the IME converts them to kana, and you confirm kanji conversions as you go. This test shows the finished Japanese sentence, so it trains the reading-and-confirming rhythm that real Japanese typing depends on, whichever input method you use.
## How to improve Japanese typing speed
Accuracy first: a missed kanji conversion costs far more time than a slow, clean sentence. Practise short daily rounds, keep your eyes on the screen, and let your fingers learn the romaji syllable rhythm — consonant plus vowel — that almost every Japanese word follows.
## WPM, CPM and Japanese
Because Japanese packs meaning into characters, one Japanese 'word' carries more content than one English word. Watch your characters per minute (CPM) alongside WPM: for Japanese, CPM is often the fairer measure of real input speed.
## Japanese typing test FAQ
Yes. It is free with no sign up, and your practice history stays on your own device.
Either works. The test shows real Japanese sentences; you reproduce the characters with your usual input method — romaji-to-kana IME, kana input, or a Japanese keyboard.

Treat it as a guide, not an absolute. Japanese words carry more meaning per character, so many typists prefer to track CPM (characters per minute), which this test also shows after every round.
Yes. Timed sentence practice with real mixed-script text builds exactly the speed and accuracy that Japanese office work and data-entry exams measure.

## Korean Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/korean-typing-test.html

Test your Korean typing speed with real Korean sentences in Hangul. Measure your speed and accuracy instantly with live results. Free, no sign up.

## Korean typing test
A Korean typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Korean sentences — everyday Hangul text with natural spacing (띄어쓰기) and punctuation. Your score appears in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so results stay comparable with the standard 1 minute typing test.
## Hangul syllable blocks and typing rhythm
Hangul is typed letter by letter — ㅎ, ㅏ, ㄴ — and the IME assembles each syllable block (한) as you go. That means Korean typing speed is really about how fast your fingers roll through the jamo inside each block. Smooth, even syllable rhythm beats short bursts of speed.
## How to improve Korean typing speed
Keep your fingers on the home row (ㅁㄴㅇㄹ / ㅏㅓㅣㅡ positions on the standard 2-set keyboard), look at the screen not the keyboard, and practise short daily rounds. Accuracy first: fixing a mis-composed syllable costs more time than typing it slowly and cleanly.
## WPM and CPM for Korean
Korean syllable blocks pack several letters into one character, so raw WPM understates the work your fingers do. Watch your characters per minute (CPM) as well: it tracks the real keystroke load of Korean text.
## Korean typing test FAQ
Yes. It is free with no sign up, and your practice history stays on your own device.
Any. The test shows real Korean sentences and measures what you produce, so the standard 2-set Hangul layout, 3-set layouts, or a mobile Korean keyboard all work.
You type individual jamo (letters) and the IME composes them into syllable blocks automatically. Fast Korean typing comes from an even jamo rhythm inside each block, not from rushing whole words.
Both are shown after each round. Because each Hangul block contains several letters, CPM (characters per minute) reflects your true keystroke speed better than WPM.
Yes. Timed sentence practice with real Hangul text builds the speed and accuracy measured in Korean office, civil-service and data-entry typing tests.

## Urdu Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/urdu-typing-test.html

Test your Urdu typing speed with real Urdu sentences in the Perso-Arabic script, typed right to left. Instant speed and accuracy results. Free, no sign up.

## Urdu typing test
An Urdu typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Urdu sentences in the Perso-Arabic (Nastaliq-style) script, written and read right to left. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so you can compare scores with the classic typing test 1 minute round.
## Right-to-left typing: what changes
The cursor moves right to left, and letters change shape depending on their position in a word — initial, medial, final or isolated forms join automatically as you type. This test renders the practice text and your input right to left, exactly as Urdu appears in real documents, so what you practise is what you produce.
## How to improve Urdu typing speed
Practise with real sentences rather than single letters, keep your eyes on the screen, and slow down at first for the characters that sit above and below the line — the diacritics and the special letters ٹ ڈ ڑ ں ہ ے. Accuracy first: rasm (spelling) mistakes cost more time than a steady, clean pace.
## Urdu typing for exams and office work
Timed Urdu passage typing is the format used in Pakistani government, court and data-entry exams, usually set in InPage or standard Urdu keyboards. Daily timed rounds with real sentences build the same speed and accuracy those tests measure — and your CPM shows the raw keystroke rate alongside WPM.
## Urdu typing test FAQ
Yes. It is free with no sign up, and your practice history stays on your own device.
Yes. Both the practice text and your input field run right to left, the way real Urdu is written and read, so your practice matches real documents.
Any standard Urdu keyboard layout — the national Urdu keyboard, phonetic layouts, or InPage-style input — because the test measures the text you produce, not the keys you press.
Yes. Urdu letters automatically take their initial, medial, final or isolated shapes as you type; the test displays the joined text exactly like any Urdu word processor.
Yes. Timed sentence practice in the Perso-Arabic script is the standard format of Pakistani government and court typing tests, so daily rounds build the same measured speed and accuracy.
